title: Testing Intelligence We Cannot Remove
summary: Starting with the ban on AI glasses in exam rooms, this essay proposes changing education and selection systems to assess the judgment and responsibility of people who will work with augmented intelligence.
content:
At next week’s college entrance exam, students will have to take off their glasses and place them on their desks if a proctor asks. Simply wearing AI glasses during the exam will invalidate their results for the year. This year’s exam must follow the agreed rules. Still, this is a scene worth remembering. The first thing a society did upon meeting a new intelligence was to make people take it off and put it on a desk.

We are a country that has selected people through exams for more than a thousand years. Even as brushes gave way to pens for machine-readable answer sheets, the principle stayed the same. Alone, empty-handed, within a set time. Drawing on what was in your head was valuable. Few people had knowledge, and proving that you did earned you a place.

That once-precious ability now fits inside a pair of glasses. On their first day at work, those who pass sit down in front of equipment far more powerful than those glasses. In the exam room, using AI disqualifies you. At work, not knowing how to use it does. More proctors can preserve only the form of the exam.

We waited more than ten years for augmented reality. It meant putting a screen in front of our eyes, and that screen was always heavy and disorienting. What actually arrived first was a pair of glasses with almost no screen. They see what I see and speak into my ear. Instead of drawing something over reality, they help the mind of the person looking at it. What has arrived before our eyes is not augmented reality but augmented intelligence.

Before long, a great many people will be wearing these glasses. Today’s glasses are a little heavy, their answers come a beat late, their batteries do not last long, and they look conspicuous. These are problems that a generation or two of products can solve. The hardest part is already inside the glasses. Just as few people with poor eyesight turn down glasses, few will turn down glasses that help them think.

Glasses are the beginning. Intelligence moved from the desk into our hands, and now it sits on our faces. Next it will touch our eyes as contact lenses, and then enter our bodies in some form connected directly to the brain. It was already twenty years ago that a person with electrodes implanted in their brain moved a cursor by thought alone. There is no reason this path should take several more decades. Five years ago, AI was at the level of stringing sentences together. Now it is beginning to do work on its own that takes people hours. On an exponential curve, measuring the next ten years by the pace of the last ten always leaves us behind.

So making people take it off has an expiration date. Glasses can be taken off and placed on a desk. Contact lenses are hard for a proctor to see. What is inside the body cannot be placed on a desk. When that day comes, how much of a person will we ask them to leave at the exam room door?

A patch that adds one more line to the list of prohibited items cannot answer this question. Education, exams, selection, and licensing all run on one operating system. At its base lies the assumption that intelligence resides inside one person’s head. That assumption has collapsed. We need a major upgrade of the entire operating system.

We must start by changing exams. We should put the energy we spend blocking this into making changes. You take the vision test for a driver’s license with your glasses on. That is because you will wear them when you drive. Exams should be taken under the conditions in which a person will actually work. Tests of basic academic skills can remain unaided. Exams that qualify people to take on work should allow augmented intelligence as early as next year.

A professional qualifying exam in 2030 might look like this. A proctor walks around the classroom checking that everyone’s glasses are on. Students who have turned theirs off are told to turn them on. The exam is one page. It contains an AI-written tax opinion with three errors hidden in it. The task is to find and correct them, explain the changes, and sign at the bottom. Anyone can get an answer. So the exam tests the eye that questions the answer and the judgment that puts a name to it. A qualification changes from proof that you know the answer to proof that you are the person who signs it. Whether intelligence resides in glasses or inside the body, the signature remains a human responsibility to the end.

There will be concerns about fairness. That is natural, since unaided exams taught us what fairness means. That version of fairness took everyone’s tools away. The fairness ahead will give everyone the same intelligence and ask them to exercise judgment on top of it. In exam rooms, we can provide the same model to everyone. In classrooms, we must put this intelligence within every student’s reach, just as we fit glasses for a child with poor eyesight. Otherwise, augmented intelligence will become a new divide.

We should also leave time in the classroom for unaided work. To notice when a machine gives a wrong answer, I need a standard in my own head. That is basic fitness. On top of that, we should teach how to think and work with augmented intelligence as a formal subject. Right now, children learn it secretly outside school.

The same model can be bought in any country. The difference emerges from the institutions that allow people to use that intelligence. Even after electricity entered factories, it took decades for productivity to rise. That was because factories had merely replaced steam engines with motors. The age of electricity truly began where factories redesigned their layouts from scratch. An exam room that collects glasses at the entrance is a factory that has only swapped in a motor.

The government is spending large sums on sovereign foundation models and AI for everyone. This is necessary. But the more fundamental work lies in our practices. It means rebuilding how we teach, assess, and select people around augmented intelligence. Which countries lead in AI will be decided on exam papers before it is decided by models. The country that completes this upgrade first will become a true AI leader. This is a time to boldly let go of yesterday’s practices and institutions.

The glasses placed on desks next week will look like confiscated objects. To me, they look like an exam paper set before our society. While we can still take them off and put them down, we have time to change our institutions. That time is short.
